objectiveEnglish: Describe food, drinks and tables at a café with ser and estar.
focusFrench: Être + adjectif pour les choses (le café est chaud) ; accord masculin/féminin et singulier/pluriel ; questions polies avec l'intonation ou est-ce que. Pour une personne : j'ai chaud/froid, jamais je suis chaud.

words.noteEnglish: Feminine: froide, as in la boisson est froide. For how you feel, say j'ai froid.
Feminine: fraîche. Le pain est frais.
Sucré is the safe word for sweet to taste. Doux means mild or soft, but can mean sweet for wine or cider.
Feminine: piquante. Épicé means spiced, not necessarily hot; for chili heat say piquant or ça pique.
The same form for both genders: libre.
French uses être for both the temporary state and the lasting quality. Très means very.
Natural spoken question with rising intonation. Est-ce que cette table est libre ? is another neutral option; inversion is more formal.
A natural way to ask about freshness today; aujourd’hui means today.

words.fr: La sauce au piment est très piquante.
words.noteEnglish: Piquante describes chili heat; the sauce in this fictional brunch scene is optional.
words.enFrenchCourse: The chili sauce is very spicy.

words.noteEnglish: A man says prêt; a woman says je suis prête.

speakingFrench: Cette table est libre ? Mon café est chaud et la sauce au piment est très piquante.

english: Daniel is at a café in Oaxaca, and many tables are taken.
Daniel asks the server: Is this table free?
The server, Rosa, says: Yes, it is free.
Daniel: Is the bread from today?
Rosa: Yes, the sweet bread is fresh.
Rosa brings coffee, orange juice and chilaquiles with salsa.
Daniel: The coffee is very hot, but the juice is cold.
Daniel: The salsa is very spicy, but it is delicious.
french: Daniel est dans un café qui sert le brunch à Lyon, et beaucoup de tables sont occupées.
Daniel demande à la serveuse : Cette table est libre ?
La serveuse, Rosa, dit : Oui, elle est libre.
Daniel : Le pain est frais aujourd’hui ?
Rosa : Oui, la brioche est fraîche.
Daniel : Je suis prêt à commander.
Rosa apporte du café, du jus d'orange, des œufs et du pain avec une sauce au piment.
Daniel : Le café est très chaud, mais le jus est froid.
Daniel : La sauce au piment est très piquante, mais elle est délicieuse.
englishFrenchCourse: Daniel is at a brunch café in Lyon, and many tables are taken.
Daniel asks the server: Is this table free?
The server, Rosa, says: Yes, it is free.
Daniel: Is the bread fresh today?
Rosa: Yes, the brioche is fresh.
Rosa brings coffee, orange juice, eggs and bread with chili sauce.
Daniel: The coffee is very hot, but the juice is cold.
Daniel: The chili sauce is very spicy, but it is delicious.

teachingNotesEnglish: French uses être to describe food and tables, with adjective agreement.
Être describes objects here. A person says j'ai chaud or j'ai froid, never je suis chaud to mean temperature.
Adjective agreement: chaud/chaude, froid/froide, frais/fraîche, occupé/occupée. Plural adds -s: occupé, occupés, occupée, occupées (les tables sont occupées).
This fictional Lyon brunch café serves eggs, bread and an optional chili sauce. Such menus vary by café.
You can ask a café question with rising intonation or est-ce que. Fixed phrases like comment allez-vous are useful now; productive inversion comes later.
FRANCE USAGE: petit-déjeuner is breakfast; in Québec, Belgium and Switzerland le déjeuner can mean breakfast.
titleFrenchCourseEnglish: Describing Food and Tables with Être
objectiveFrenchCourseEnglish: Describe food, drinks and available tables in French with être and adjective agreement.
speakingInstructionEnglish: Ask a server if a table is free, then describe whether your coffee is hot or cold and whether the chili sauce is spicy.
focusEnglish: Describe objects with être and adjective agreement; ask natural café questions with intonation or est-ce que. For how a person feels, say j'ai chaud or j'ai froid.
